analysis.title: A Looming Profit Squeeze
key_insights: TS Lombard (Freya Beamish) says the US labour market is clearly reaccelerating, with total NFP employment up 165K in October. The reacceleration spans manufacturing and services.
Manufacturing employment continues to strengthen. Total imports have taken off because of AI, which was untariffed, while import penetration in other sectors has receded.
The broadening of profit growth appears centred on datacentres. Datacentre construction may create direct spillovers, though construction employment was one of the few decliners last month.
The wider driver of labour demand is expected to be real income growth picking up from the mid-year trough, especially if energy prices are contained.
Wage growth is likely bottoming. Excluding education and health it has already bottomed, and job-to-job moves show wages accelerating, which tends to lead the broader market.
Measured productivity growth could deteriorate as the labour market reaccelerates, so unit labour cost (ULC) growth should start to rise. The report concludes aggregate profit growth faces headwinds.

Tech may face disappointment too, and the report points to Dario's macro pictures. A continued tech sell-off could reverse wealth effects and hit demand, though the report expects any such slowdown to be temporary.
The UK is cited as an economy where the cyclical profits story is less advanced: the labour market is slack, wage growth is falling and productivity is surprising to the upside.
The reacceleration reinforces TS Lombard's call for Fed hikes beyond insurance against energy inflation. The report says Q1 will not be the last hike.
Falling energy prices return purchasing power to consumers and support labour demand while labour supply stays constrained.

sector_views.rationale: Tech may face disappointment, and a continued tech sell-off could reverse wealth effects. The report cites datacentres as the centre of profit broadening.

earnings_insights: The report expects aggregate profit growth to face headwinds as unit labour cost growth rises. It gives no company-level EPS or revenue figures.

macro_indicators.indicator: US total nonfarm payroll employment change
macro_indicators.interpretation: The report reads this as clear labour market reacceleration, which supports its call for further Fed hikes.
Rising ULC growth would squeeze aggregate profit growth.
Wage growth excluding education and health has already bottomed, and job-to-job moves point to acceleration.

macro_indicators.reading: Further hikes expected, Q1 will not be the last hike
macro_indicators.interpretation: The report says hikes are not only insurance against energy inflation.

risk_factors: Continued tech sell-off reversing wealth effects and weakening demand.
Rising unit labour costs squeezing aggregate profit growth.
Productivity growth deteriorating as the labour market reaccelerates.
Energy prices staying elevated, which would limit real income growth.

key_data_points.metric: US total NFP employment change, October
key_data_points.context: October payrolls, cited as evidence the labour market is clearly reaccelerating
key_data_points.anchor: total NFP employment rose 165K in October

tension_points.bull_case: The reacceleration is broad across manufacturing and services. Real income growth is expected to pick up from the mid-year trough, and profit growth is broadening, centred on datacentres.
tension_points.bear_case: Wage growth is bottoming and productivity may deteriorate, so unit labour costs should rise and squeeze aggregate profits. Tech may disappoint.
tension_points.what_invalidates: A continued tech sell-off reversing wealth effects would threaten demand, though the report expects any slowdown to be temporary.

theme_stances.evidence: ULC growth will start picking up again, suggesting less favourable aggregate profit growth

theme_stances.key_argument: Labour market reacceleration reinforces the call for Fed hikes beyond insurance against energy inflation.
theme_stances.evidence: We stand by our call that Fed hikes are not just about energy
